summary: Defines a Telnet option that lets one side ask the other to echo back what it receives. It is an Internet Standard.

eli5.summary: When you type, either your computer or the far one repeats the letters on screen. This option decides who does it.

questions: what is the telnet echo option
why does telnet need suppress go ahead with echo
subtitle: How the two ends of a Telnet connection agree on who repeats typed characters back to the screen.

tldr.problem: A Telnet terminal normally echoes typed characters locally, but in highly interactive situations the remote process wants to control how characters are echoed.
tldr.mechanism: The ECHO option (code 1) uses the Telnet WILL, WON'T, DO and DON'T commands so each direction of the connection can independently agree to echo or not.
tldr.outcome: Echo is off by default, each direction is switched on and off separately, and both ends must never echo for each other or characters would bounce back and forth forever.

today: RFC 857 is an Internet Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why an Echo Option Exists
sections.content:
The Network Virtual Terminal (NVT) has a keyboard and a printer that are nominally wired together, so characters typed on the keyboard are turned around locally and printed. Echoes never need to cross the network.

In highly interactive situations the remote process, such as a command language interpreter, should control how characters are echoed. The ECHO option lets the two ends of the Telnet connection agree that characters typed on an NVT keyboard are echoed by the party at the other end.
sections.eli5: Normally your own screen shows what you type. Sometimes the far computer wants to be the one that shows it, so they need a way to agree.

sections.title: The Four Commands
sections.content:
The option has code 1 and uses the four standard negotiation commands:

  • IAC WILL ECHO: the sender requests to begin, or confirms it will begin, echoing the data characters it receives.
  • IAC WON'T ECHO: the sender demands to stop, or refuses to start, echoing.
  • IAC DO ECHO: the sender requests that the receiver begin echoing, or confirms the receiver is expected to echo.
  • IAC DON'T ECHO: the sender demands that the receiver stop, or not start, echoing.

The default is WON'T ECHO and DON'T ECHO: no echoing is done over the connection.
sections.eli5: Each side can say 'I will repeat your letters' or 'please repeat mine', and the other side can say yes or no. If nobody asks, nobody repeats.

sections.title: How Echo Mode Works
sections.content:
When echo is in effect, the party doing the echoing is expected to send back the data characters it receives. They need not be exactly the same characters; the RFC notes that a number of systems echo the ASCII ESC character with something other than ESC. When echo is not in effect, the receiver should not echo, though it may still respond to what it receives.

Each direction of a Telnet connection is independent, so neither, either or both directions may be in echo mode. The RFC lists five reasonable modes: neither end echoes, one end echoes for itself, one end echoes for the other, both ends echo for themselves, and one end echoes for both ends. The option only decides whether either end echoes for the other; whether an end echoes for itself is left to the systems at each end.

If both hosts echo the characters sent by the other, any character is echoed back and forth indefinitely, so an implementation must not allow echoing to be turned on at one site while the other is echoing. Either party may later demand a return to non-echo mode, and each direction must be removed from echo mode separately. Mode switches should be timed precisely: if a party answers DO ECHO with WILL ECHO, the WILL ECHO should immediately precede the first echoed character.
sections.eli5: If two parrots each repeat what the other says, they never stop. So only one side may repeat, and the computers must be careful not to set up a loop.

sections.title: Using It With Suppress Go Ahead
sections.content:
The ECHO option alone will normally not give what people think of as remote echoing of typed characters. The SUPPRESS-GO-AHEAD option will normally have to be used together with it to get character-at-a-time remote echoing.

The RFC also sketches a simple user system, called UHOST, that keeps three state bits per terminal: Physical (does the terminal echo for itself), Desired (the user's preference) and Actual (the state of the connection). It sends DO ECHO when the minimum of the first two differs from the third. The RFC adds that a large server may switch modes often, for example sending WON'T ECHO during line-at-a-time work and WILL ECHO during character-at-a-time work.
sections.eli5: To make every letter show up the moment you type it, you need two settings turned on together: this one and the 'no taking turns' one.
